summary: Describes using keys derived from an IKEv2 security association as the shared secret for OWAMP and TWAMP, which allows certificate-based key exchange and gives more operational flexibility.

plainLanguage.summary: OWAMP and TWAMP are the protocols used to measure how a network performs: they send probe packets and time them. The measurements are only worth anything if the results cannot be faked, which needs a shared secret between the two ends. This RFC shows how to derive that secret from an existing IKEv2 security association, so operators do not have to hand out and manage a separate passphrase for every measurement endpoint.

subtitle: Deriving the shared secret for network measurement from an IKEv2 security association.

tldr.problem: OWAMP and TWAMP measure how a network performs by sending probe packets and timing them, and the measurements are worthless unless they cannot be tampered with. The protocols require a shared secret at both ends, but only support a pre-shared key, which means provisioning and managing a passphrase for every measurement endpoint.
tldr.mechanism: The shared secret is derived from the key of an existing IKEv2 security association with the formula prf(SK_d, "IPPM"). The client puts the association identifiers in the KeyID field of the Set-Up-Response, the server looks up the same association, and both ends compute the same secret without exchanging it.
tldr.outcome: Measurement endpoints that already run IKEv2 no longer need a separately managed passphrase, so certificate-based key exchange and automatic key management become available to OWAMP and TWAMP. A new mode bit, IKEv2Derived, lets the server advertise the capability, and older clients ignore it.

facts.label: Shared secret derivation
facts.value: prf(SK_d, "IPPM"), with the label in ASCII

facts.label: Token contents
facts.value: a 16-octet Challenge, a 16-octet AES session key and a 32-octet HMAC-SHA1 session key

facts.label: SPI length
facts.value: 8 octets each, for SPIi and SPIr

today: RFC 7717 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2015. It updates RFC 4656 and RFC 5357, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or further updates it. The companion document for the OWAMP modes registry is RFC 7718.

sections.title: The Problem with Shared Passphrases
sections.content:
The One-Way Active Measurement Protocol and the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol measure network performance parameters such as latency, bandwidth and packet loss by sending probe packets and watching what happens to them in the network. The security of those measurements has to be considered, or the results can be attacked: an adversary in the middle may modify packet timestamps and so alter the measurement.

Both protocols require that the endpoints, the client and the server, hold a shared secret. In today's deployments the use of pre-shared keys is far from optimal. In wireless infrastructure networks, some network elements support certificate-based security: think of measuring IP performance between an E-UTRAN Evolved Node B and a Security Gateway, both of which are 3GPP Long Term Evolution nodes that support certificate mode and the Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2 (IKEv2).

The O/TWAMP security mechanism supports the pre-shared key mode only, which hinders large-scale deployment, because provisioning and managing shared secrets for massive deployments consumes a tremendous amount of effort and is prone to human error. With IKEv2 widely deployed, deriving the shared key from an IKEv2 security association is a viable alternative. O/TWAMP can then support certificate-based key exchange, which increases operational flexibility and makes automatic key management easier to extend.

The document specifies a method for network measurements between a TWAMP client and a TWAMP server. Implementations signal the use of the method by setting the IKEv2Derived mode, and IKEv2-derived keys SHOULD be used instead of shared secrets when O/TWAMP is employed in a deployment using IKEv2.
sections.plainLanguage: Measuring a network means sending probe packets and timing them. For the numbers to be worth anything, the two ends need a secret that only they know, so that nobody in between can rewrite the timestamps. This RFC says where to get that secret from: the security association that IKEv2 already sets up.

sections.title: How O/TWAMP Security Works Today
sections.content:
O/TWAMP uses a simple cryptographic protocol: AES-CBC for confidentiality and HMAC-SHA1 truncated to 128 bits for message authentication. The OWAMP-Control protocol supports three modes, unauthenticated, authenticated and encrypted, and the TWAMP-Control protocol adds a mixed mode in which the control protocol is encrypted while the test protocol is unauthenticated. The authenticated, encrypted and mixed modes require that the endpoints hold a shared secret, typically a passphrase, and the secret key is derived from that passphrase with PBKDF2.

The control connection starts with a TCP connection from the Control-Client to the Server. The Server answers with a Server Greeting containing the Modes, Challenge, Salt, Count and MBZ fields. If the client's preferred mode is available, the client replies with a Set-Up-Response that carries the selected Mode, the KeyID, the Token and the client initialization vector. The Token is the concatenation of a 16-octet Challenge, a 16-octet AES session key for encryption and a 32-octet HMAC-SHA1 session key for authentication, and it is encrypted with AES-CBC. The Server answers with a Server-Start carrying the Server-IV. From then on each side encrypts with its own IV, and the IVs themselves travel in cleartext.

The test protocol runs over UDP using the session numbers negotiated during the Request-Session exchange. Each test session has its own AES and HMAC session keys, but instead of being generated afresh they are derived from the control session keys together with the 16-octet session identifier. That makes the shared secret the root of the whole scheme, and for large deployments, provisioning and managing that root is exactly what becomes unwieldy.
sections.plainLanguage: The measurement protocols already have a security scheme: encrypt the control and test packets, and add a message authentication code. What it lacks is a good source of the shared secret, which today has to be a passphrase copied to both ends and then stretched into a key.

sections.title: Deriving the Shared Secret from IKEv2
sections.content:
In the authenticated, encrypted and mixed modes the shared secret key MUST be derived from the IKEv2 SA. The document derives it from the IKEv2 SA rather than the child SA, because an IKEv2 SA can be created without generating any child SA.

When the shared secret is derived from the IKEv2 SA, SK_d has to be generated first, computed as specified in RFC 7296. The shared secret key is then generated as prf(SK_d, "IPPM"), where the string "IPPM" is encoded in ASCII and prf is a pseudorandom function.

It is recommended that the shared secret key be derived in the IPsec layer, so that IPsec keying material is not exposed to the O/TWAMP client. The interaction between the O/TWAMP and IPsec layers is internal to the host and implementation specific, so it is outside the scope of the document. One possible arrangement is that the IPsec layer on the Control-Client side looks up the IKEv2 SA in the Security Association Database using the Server's IP address, while on the Server side it looks up the IKEv2 SA using the Security Parameter Indexes sent by the Control-Client.

If both ends support IKEv2 but there is no current IKEv2 SA, there are two alternatives: the Control-Client starts establishing the IKEv2 SA, logs the operation and selects the mode that supports IKEv2, or it does not start the establishment, logs an error for operational management and proceeds with the modes defined in the earlier O/TWAMP specifications. If the IKEv2 SA is rekeyed or deleted, the shared secret key derived from it MUST continue to be used until the O/TWAMP session terminates.
sections.plainLanguage: The derivation is one step: take the IKEv2 association key, run it through a pseudorandom function with a fixed label, and the result is the shared secret both ends will use. Because the two ends already run IKEv2, each can work the key out for itself instead of having it delivered.

sections.title: Telling the Other End That IKEv2 Is Used
sections.content:
To trigger a binding between the key generated from IKEv2 and the O/TWAMP shared secret key, the Modes field in the Server Greeting must support key derivation as described above. Support for deriving the shared key from the IKEv2 SA is indicated by setting the IKEv2Derived mode bit, and when this method is used the Modes value extension MUST be supported.

The choice of Modes values poses no backwards-compatibility problem. Robust legacy Control-Client implementations disregard the fact that the IKEv2Derived bit is set in the Server Greeting. A Control-Client implementing this method can also tell that the server it contacted does not support the specification, and can then choose another mode, or simply behave as a client compatible with the earlier specifications.

The IANA registry of TWAMP modes was reformatted for this document as a set of single-bit positions. The bits already assigned are 0 for Unauthenticated, 1 for Authenticated, 2 for Encrypted, 3 for the mixed mode of an unauthenticated test protocol with an encrypted control protocol, 4 for Individual Session Control, 5 for Reflect Octets Capability and 6 for the symmetrical size sender test packet format. This document adds bit 7, the IKEv2Derived Mode Capability.
sections.plainLanguage: The server says in its greeting that it can do this, by setting one extra bit in a field that lists the security modes it supports. A client that does not know the bit simply ignores it, so old and new clients can both talk to the same server.

sections.title: Carrying the IKEv2 Association in the KeyID
sections.content:
The Security Parameter Index uniquely identifies a security association. If the Control-Client supports shared secret key derivation for the IKEv2 SA, it chooses the corresponding Mode value and carries SPIi and SPIr in the KeyID field. SPIi and SPIr MUST be included in the KeyID field of the Set-Up-Response to say which IKEv2 SA the O/TWAMP shared secret key was derived from. The length of an SPI is 8 octets, so the first 8 octets of the KeyID field MUST carry SPIi and the second 8 octets MUST carry SPIr. The remaining bits of the KeyID field MUST be set to zero.

An O/TWAMP Server implementation MUST obtain SPIi and SPIr from the first 16 octets and ignore the remaining octets of the KeyID field, and the client and server can then derive the shared secret key from the Mode value and the SPIs. If the server cannot find the IKEv2 SA corresponding to the SPIi and SPIr it received, it MUST log the event for operational management purposes, and it SHOULD set the Accept field of the Server-Start message to the value 6 to say that it is not willing to conduct further transactions in this O/TWAMP-Control session.
sections.plainLanguage: The client has to tell the server which security association to use, because both ends may have several. It puts the two association identifiers at the start of a field the message already has, and the server looks that association up, works out the same shared secret, and both sides now agree on the same keys without exchanging them.

sections.title: Measuring Inside an IPsec Tunnel
sections.content:
In general, O/TWAMP measurement packets can be transmitted inside the IPsec tunnel, as typical user traffic is, or outside it. Which one applies depends on the operator's policy and on the performance evaluation goal, and it is orthogonal to the key derivation method. When IPsec is deployed, protecting O/TWAMP traffic in unauthenticated mode using IPsec is one option. Another is to protect the traffic with the O/TWAMP security built on the key derived from IKEv2 and to bypass the IPsec tunnel.

Protecting unauthenticated O/TWAMP control and test traffic with the Authentication Header or the Encapsulating Security Payload cannot provide every security option that O/TWAMP wants, for example authenticating part of an O/TWAMP packet. Latency measurement carries a timestamp in the test traffic, and the sender has to fetch the timestamp, encrypt it and send it. With the method in this document, partial authentication of O/TWAMP packets is possible, so the middle step can be skipped: the sequence number can be encrypted and authenticated before the timestamp is fetched, and the receiver obtains the timestamp without a separate decryption step. That can improve accuracy.

The IPsec Authentication Header and Encapsulating Security Payload give confidentiality and data integrity to IP datagrams, and an IPsec tunnel can provide the protection needed for O/TWAMP control and test packets even when the peers choose the unauthenticated mode. To ensure authenticity and security, O/TWAMP packets between two IKEv2 systems SHOULD be configured to use the corresponding IPsec tunnel running over an external network even when the O/TWAMP unauthenticated mode is in use.
sections.plainLanguage: Measurement traffic can go through the IPsec tunnel or outside it. The RFC points out one advantage of going outside: the sender can protect and check the sequence number before it fetches the timestamp, which saves a step and can make the timing more accurate.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: As the shared secret key is derived from the IKEv2 SA, the key derivation algorithm's strength and limitations are those of RFC 7296. The strength of a key derived from a Diffie-Hellman exchange depends on the inherent strength of the group, the size of the exponent used, and the entropy provided by the random number generator employed. The strength of all keys, and the implementation vulnerabilities, in particular denial-of-service attacks, are as defined in RFC 7296.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC passes the security question on to IKEv2: the derived key is exactly as strong as the Diffie-Hellman exchange underneath it, so the group, the exponent size and the quality of the random number generator all matter.

messages.label: TCP CONNECTION
messages.note: The client opens the connection so it can send control commands.

messages.label: GREETING MESSAGE
messages.note: Carries the Modes, Challenge, Salt, Count and MBZ fields.

messages.note: Carries the selected Mode, the KeyID, the Token and the Client-IV.

viz.caption: THE CHAIN OF KEYS UNDER ONE MEASUREMENT SESSION

items.title: SK_d
items.text: The key of the IKEv2 security association, computed as in RFC 7296.

items.title: Shared secret key
items.text: prf(SK_d, "IPPM"). The root secret that protects the session keys.

items.title: AES Session-key
items.text: 16 octets, generated randomly by the Control-Client for the control session.

items.title: HMAC Session-key
items.text: 32 octets, generated randomly and sent inside the Token, used to authenticate messages.

items.title: Test session keys
items.text: Derived from the control session keys together with the 16-octet session identifier.

data.title: Shared secret key derivation
data.code:
Shared secret key = prf( SK_d, "IPPM" )

SK_d  : the key of the IKEv2 security association
prf  : a pseudorandom function
IPPM : the label, encoded in ASCII

items.label: Unauthenticated
items.desc: The security parameters are left unused.

items.label: Mixed mode
items.desc: The control protocol is encrypted while the test protocol is unauthenticated.

items.label: IKEv2Derived
items.desc: Set in the Server Greeting to say the shared key is derived from an IKEv2 security association.

fields.name: Mode
fields.desc: The selected security mode, with the IKEv2Derived bit set.

fields.name: KeyID
fields.desc: 80 octets. The first 8 carry SPIi and the next 8 carry SPIr; the rest must be zero.

fields.name: Token
fields.desc: 16 octets: the Challenge, the AES session key and the HMAC session key, encrypted with AES-CBC.

fields.name: Client-IV
fields.desc: 12 octets. The initialization vector for the client side of the connection.
